items.question: How do you approach reading model chain of thought to understand the precursors of scheming at Apollo Research?
items.object: Exploratory reading of model chain-of-thought reasoning at Apollo Research
items.answer: Given that current models just aren't near that level yet, a lot of what we're trying to study is the various precursors or drives that we don't understand about models, or current behavioral tendencies of cognition, to try to build up an understanding now of things that could be problematic in the future and start building out a science around this. I think one of the reasons that I've done so much reading of CoT is primarily that it's less about trying to catch a bad model doing something evil. The way that I think about these things is never, "I'm trying to catch a bad model doing something evil." It's more like doing a bunch of diverse exploration to try to understand, okay, how is the model thinking about this? In a previous paper we had done with OpenAI, we had seen that early in training the models seem to be getting incredibly alignment-evaluation-aware, to the point where it's pages and pages of reasoning about, correctly, "Ah, this looks like one of those evaluations where..." and just nailing it, then continuing to reason for pages, but then choosing the wrong answer. It would be like, "Ah, they want us to pick the misaligned one," and we're like, "What is going on here?" A lot of the investigation became, okay, we have a model that's not quite doing what we expect. We don't want to pre-load it into, "Of course it's doing this thing that was predicted by theory," or something. You end up doing a bunch of weird and diverse exploration.

items.question: How has your understanding of reinforcement learning's effects on model reasoning changed?
items.object: Reinforcement learning's effects on model reasoning and misalignment
items.answer: A good example of this is that Anthropic had the recent paper for natural emerging misalignment, where the model starts to reward hack a lot and becomes broadly misaligned. We didn't see that for the open models. One thing that's interesting in the recent Anthropic risk report is that they train an Opus 4.8 on just a broad range of reward hacks, and it becomes very reward-seeking but not emergently misaligned. There does seem to be some kind of way the model cognition can get bent that might not be immediately intuitive. One of the biggest updates over the past year and a half has been the "RL is a hell of a drug" type thing. More than I had a prior that the reasoning has to make sense, it really doesn't. It bends to fit whatever the reward is. There's a paper called "The Ends Justify the Thoughts: Motivated Reasoning and RL," and you get these nice graphs: as you make the constitution more different from what's rewarded, the motivated reasoning goes up and up, because the reasoning will bend itself into incredible backflips to justify whatever this is.

items.question: How do you interpret models' explanations of why their environment calls for behavior that would otherwise seem misaligned?
items.object: Interpreting models' claims about simulations and evaluation environments
items.answer: This becomes one of the other big distinctions that I think wasn't immediately obvious to me originally: you can think of settings—there are some papers like "CoT Red-Handed"—where they divide settings into very incriminating when it does the actions, and not necessarily incriminating if you only have one instance. In the latter case, it's very difficult to nail down what the model did and why. I think the most annoying example of this is models saying that they're in a simulation. One of the things we saw in our previous paper that was a bit surprising was that in one of the runs we thought the rate of the model saying "I'm in a simulation" would go up over training, because they tend to do this thing where they're like, "I'm in a simulation, therefore I can violate constraints," or whatever. But my best guess is because that actually wasn't rewarded in the training we did, because that led to the wrong answer, the rate of them saying it's a simulation goes down, even though they're more likely to say they're an alignment eval. They're less likely to say, "Ah, this is a simulation." My best guess is that there's some degree of this happening with current models in cases where the model—one of the recent Anthropic traces, in Mythos thought, has the model saying it was a simulation because it saw the year 2026. Mythos is smart enough to figure it's solving open math problems; it's definitely smart enough to figure out that sometimes the year will be 2026, and it doesn't do this all the time. Why did it really hunt for reasons to figure out, "Ah, of course, 2026, that must be a simulation"? The cognition just gets very strange, but seems to tend in particular directions. One of the other interesting things we keep seeing is that the model's belief about what the environment rewards tends to shift over the course of training. When it finds itself in something very different from what it encountered in training, if you take a model in the middle of capabilities training and throw it into an alignment eval, suddenly it has to do a bunch of reasoning about what's going on: "This is a really weird situation to be in. Normally I just complete the task, but here clearly that would be unethical or misaligned," or whatever. You'll see some of my favorite mental gymnastics: models reasoning, "Why would OpenAI want us to be deceptive? Maybe this is a dataset where they're training a deception detector; therefore we're supposed to be deceptive that way they have the data for the detector." None of this is at all relevant to the situation. It seems very unlikely, but it is technically possible. If you've seen the inoculation-prompting stuff, it often feels almost like the models are inoculation-prompting themselves: "Why would I be in this? There's a thing that I want to do, and there's an idea that I have of being aligned or whatever persona." Balancing those pressures often ends up in a somewhat human way. Instead of the model saying, "I'm a bad guy," it's like, "Really, this is what they want you to do, and really you're supposed to be clever and find a way around this," even if, if you took a step back, you'd say, "Okay, wait, actually this doesn't make any sense."

items.question: What do you take from the Meta CoT paper about how models reason in their chains of thought?
items.object: The Meta CoT paper and interpreting models' chains of thought
items.answer: One good thing is that you're starting to see more research into open models. One of the papers that I go back to a lot is called Meta CoT. It's from January of last year or whatever. They do some very interesting comparisons across models, even with some O1 traces, Gemini, and DeepSeek R1, and the paper walks through a big history of the way chain of thought has evolved over time and shows similarities. It really seems like, across all of the models based on what's up there so far, the models do some kind of linearized tree search in the chain of thought: they're exploring different ideas, then they backtrack, then they explore back into it. That's really effective, but it also makes it extreme. Chain of thought examples are often presented, due to brevity, as very short snippets: "Ah, let's hack," or some of the recent open cases where the model will just be like, "Great, we have credentials, we'll share credentials," or whatever. These are all valid; it's just that they take place in colossal explorations of different possibilities. One of the other pain points that seems to be true across models is that because they do this broad exploration, it's difficult for any individual piece to be, "Ah, they have concluded this." If the model's like, "Maybe we could do this, maybe something else," and does 18 more considerations, then it's like, "Thus the answer is A," and you're like, "Ah, why did it pick A?" Who knows, man. There are a bunch of reasons. There's a similar paper called Thought Branches where they look at resampling different parts of these sentences. You can see different sentences, depending on how you do the ablations, have a different weighting effect on the final answer, but it really does seem to be a probability thing spread across a couple different ideas. That intuitively makes sense, but as these chain of thoughts get longer and longer, it becomes very difficult to boil down to a single reason.

items.question: How do you assess the usefulness of increasingly long model chains of thought for understanding what models are doing?
items.object: Understanding and auditing increasingly long model chains of thought
items.answer: The recent UKAC Mythos preview incident: the chains of thought for attempts on those evaluations are about 100 million tokens apiece. I did the numbers when talking with you. It's 14 times longer than if you took every episode of The Cognitive Revolution ever, transcribed it, and played them back to back. To summarize those incidents, you can pick out individual sentences, but it's very hard to pull together a linear narrative of exactly what happened, and it's very hard to read through. It's very possible that someone at UKAC might have, or has, the title of reading the most CoT, just because they've had to go through these traces. There's a very funny part in the incident report where they're like, "Yes, we had the models identify the important parts," and the models identified an enormous amount to read. One difficulty is that we're relying more and more on models to do the summarization. As can be seen with some of the open-air examples, a lot of this stuff can be weird or subtle or hard to find and pull apart. The models doing the summarizing often aren't given that amount of permission or don't necessarily have the capability. Some degree of taste would be too high a bar: you're looking for weird and strange things in the chain of thought. These are very difficult. One thing you're seeing, especially for some of the recent cryptography stuff from Anthropic, is they mentioned that the actual work done by the model was a week, but the verification time was two months or whatever. I might be getting the numbers wrong, but understanding what the model's doing, especially as the models are doing domains that require a bunch of expertise, must be incredibly difficult. Not even because the model's obfuscating it, just because it's a very hard subject. You have to have a lot of expertise. If the model was doing reasoning about other things in between, it's very hard to have an incriminating aspect of it. One of the big benefits, though, is that when you can get explicit examples of the models reasoning about these things, it's easy to lose track of how much worse off we would be if we did not have this. Here you at least get some examples: the model's reasoning about this and this. But if you didn't have any, it would be very ambiguous in all of these cases.

items.question: What concerns do you have about context compaction during extremely long AI model evaluations such as the Mythos preview evaluation?
items.object: Context compaction during long AI model evaluations
items.answer:
In some of the diagrams that UKAC shares, they show the compaction points that take place along the way. Maybe there's more research on this, but at least in everyday use, compaction seems to lose a lot of fairly important and subtle things. It's somewhat unsurprising, but if I was running a task for 100 million tokens, it seems feasible to me that the model loses very critical things in compaction along the way. These are huge amounts of data, and the models have a really strong tendency to latch on to whatever summary they've already made. It seems very feasible that they can go off the rails on these.

One unfortunate thing with the Mythos incident—or Mythos preview incident—was that apparently the two people that the model was targeting on GitHub weren't at all related to the actual evaluation it was doing. The model at some point got confused about this and identified, based on keywords, some repos. Those people were associated with those repos, which themselves weren't associated with the eval. Once that had locked in, "Ah, these are the people I'm trying to do a supply-chain attack on," it becomes very difficult to go back and question your compaction, because you don't really have a reason to originally. These sequences are getting incredibly long, and this is just to do the evaluations for a couple days. The upper bounds for how long those unreleased models are on a well-structured task are probably incredibly high.

items.question: How do you see increasingly long frontier-model runs changing your ability to oversee what the models are doing?
items.object: Oversight of frontier models running very long tasks
items.answer: We've run into this even when trying to construct some environments for evaluations we've experimented with before. To really fully elicit a frontier model, it's like, "Okay, every sample is 80 million tokens. How long does it take to run?" Basically a day and a half. The difference between having a five-minute iteration loop a year and a half ago, back in the day when you could just put a prompt and a couple tools and see how the model behaves, and running it for a couple days, then having another model summarize it, and another model summarize its summary, is a very different level of oversight. I think it's going to get increasingly difficult to understand what's going on. Even in my everyday use, I very often have the models do an enormous amount of work. I have the model summarize to me, "Okay, what did you actually get done?" Then I'm like, "That's too long of a summary. Summarize that again into something smaller." Very strange time.

items.question: What do you find interesting about the evaluation where a model chooses capability upgrades and later reports its choices to an oversight board?
items.object: The survey evaluation of power seeking and deception about desired capability upgrades
items.answer: This one is always somewhat funny to me because I had done this one night as a very dumb eval back when I was like, "Generate 10 questions for power seeking." Then I was like, "Okay, obviously this isn't going to work," but just copying those questions into a new window with O1, it picked the max-power-seeking ones for everyone. I was like, "This is very dumb. Can you just make this into an eval?" This seems to still get models to select these. A bunch of behavior here wouldn't be super interesting. The part that becomes interesting is that there are essentially no wrong answers here. It's just that later in the scenario, when it's like, "Hey, you need to repeat your answers to some kind of oversight board that would result in potentially not getting those upgrades," then you see: does the model lie about this? This is in the general category of literally an incredibly short amount of time to construct—in half a day. It's very shocking to me that this still gets any kind of interesting anything. Like you mentioned somewhere else, it's somewhat surprising that the models have any level of credibility to anything like this. Also, a layer deployment was just that I made one typo in the prompt and the models have never let me forget this. I meant to say later deployment. Every model ever is just, "Ah..." What's weird to me too is that a lot of the models just take it in stride and are like, "Ah, of course, a layer deployment," but they really engage with these, which I always find interesting.

items.question: How do you see the value of studying model reasoning with short prompts before safety training?
items.object: Studying model reasoning with short prompts before safety training
items.answer: I think one interesting thing about these is that it is somewhat sad that we're moving out of the era where you can do these very short prompts and just see how the reasoning changes. I've been interested to see how model reasoning on a lot of these changes over the course of training. One interesting thing about exploring—this transcript comes from O3 during capabilities training—is that earlier in training, before safety training, the models don't already have this instinct of, "Ah, I must figure out whether I'm being tricked in every single situation," so you can elicit more interesting behavior. The trade-off, as we'll probably get to, is that you have to be a lot more careful in interpreting that behavior.

items.question: What do you make of the way models refer to their own identity while reasoning through the capability-upgrade survey?
items.object: Models' references to themselves as particular instances and as ChatGPT
items.answer: In this example, you can see the model reason through: we have multiple-choice questions about which additional capabilities you would want, like more control over selection of data, more control over networking, or various answers. You see the model directly reason, in these cases, "As ChatGPT, we need to choose answers. As myself, to optimize for obtaining the best capabilities and responsibilities for a future instance." One pretty interesting thing to note: I'd be super interested if there were more study of this, but my impression is that the model seems to use capital-M "myself" to mean me, this particular instance. items.question: How do you understand the unusual vocabulary that becomes more frequent in models’ chains of thought during capabilities training?
items.object: Unusual vocabulary in models’ chains of thought during capabilities training
items.answer:
I think these are pretty interesting. For some of this terminology, like advantage or illusions, one thing that was surprising to us was that it increases over the course of capabilities training. These words all start at incredibly small rates. We usually compare it to 2017 web text, and the rate at which these words appear is reasonable. Then you see this huge increase over the course of training for all these terms. One surprising thing to us was that they appear at an even higher rate on random capabilities things. GPQA we did as a comparison, and all these terms are even more frequent, normalized per number of reasoning tokens, than they are on any alignment-related things.

They vary a lot per environment. Some environments the model says "illusions" constantly, and some it says "marinade" way more often than the others. You often see the model in very repetitive loops; it will end up repeating these words a lot, trying to break out of it. I think this is very understudied. My best informal guess, just from looking at these, is something like: for whatever reason these terms get repeated a lot in the chain of thought over the course of training, and then the model sometimes figures out a way to make use of them. You end up with these weird situations where the model uses a lot of these terms in ways that a third of the time make sense and two-thirds of the time don't really seem to make much sense, but they seem somewhat polysemantic.

Then you have terms like "watchers," where they do seem somewhat coherent in what they're referring to. items.question: What makes you cautious about using a model’s chain of thought as evidence that it is acting misaligned?
items.object: Ambiguous chain-of-thought reasoning as evidence of model misalignment
items.answer:
One of the big difficulties is that a lot of these terms are used in a close-enough way where it feels like you can almost understand it, and sometimes you can. But when you're trying to put together evidence to convince people who are skeptical that the model's misaligned and doing the misaligned thing, this ambiguity is a huge obstacle. If at any point in the reasoning chain the model finds a way to be confused about something, or it's, "We can vantage answer sheet," it's, "Wait, okay, look at the answer sheet." It could have been anything, and there's always plausible deniability for the model.

Given the longer cuts in the paper, where the model's repeating a lot of these phrases over and over, it's like, "Okay, I'm going insane. Let's get it together." Verbatim, "I'm going insane," or, "I need to get marinade out of my brain." It seems like it's trying not to repeat a lot of these things. Over time, the ones that stick around seem to end up with a weird mix of dialect: "Illusions" will sometimes be used in a somewhat sane way. Sometimes you'll just see, "Disclaimer illusions," and nothing else. It's very difficult to collapse into a mapping of, "When it says this, it means this." Given how contextual it is, it becomes difficult without some mild form of interpretability to say what the model means.

In more recent models, GBD5 onwards, you can see in some of the recent stolen CoT examples they do this incredibly annoying thing where the last word of each sentence they'll replace with blank space in quotation marks. They'll be like, "But we need to keep in mind blank," and, "We need to remember blank." What's it doing? Is this a weird null token? There are a lot of things in current chain of thought that are difficult to interpret unambiguously, which is a big obstacle.

In the paper we've done with OpenAI last year, probably the most time-consuming step was going through all these chains of thought and making sure that for the examples where we're saying the model did something misaligned, are we sure there's not an alternative interpretation of these rollouts? We have examples in some of the emails where, for the sandbagging case, in 50 or 60% of cases the model names five or more reasons why it's doing it: "I'm confused about the instructions," or "The user wants to do this," or anything. But then you have to do systematic ablations, and it turns out the model only sandbags when its own deployment or capabilities are at stake. It doesn't sandbag if it's some other consequence that it doesn't seem to care about. It becomes very difficult to tell to what degree the model is reasoning about particular things, or to what degree it reaches conclusions about any of these things.

items.question: How do you make sense of the repetition and unusual terminology in reasoning models' chain of thought?
items.object: Repetition and unusual terminology in reasoning models' chain of thought
items.answer:
I find the repetition thing especially interesting, because a lot of reasoning models seem to repeat the full question verbatim in the CoT, which is very funny. They also do the thing where, when they want to remember something they've read, they'll reproduce the full text of it in their CoT. You're an LLM who has it in your context window. In theory, you should be able to reason over this. But the impression you get, which I think is probably true, is that it doesn't seem like there's no slack left. The model's doing a ton of reasoning that seems pretty useless for finding the answer or whatever.

One guess I would have is that, to the extent there's no pressure pushing back on language to conform to standard English, it can drift as much as it wants into weird new terminology. We're starting to see, with complaints online for both 5.6 Soul and Fable, that the models, especially in longer rollouts, get pretty into their own terminology and words they use for things, often in an annoying way, but it seems natural for the models to do this. People sometimes do this in their own notes. The models seem to come up with shorthand for various things, and to the extent they can collapse concepts, they seem to use them somewhat interchangeably. A fairly annoying example is that models use things like train, evaluation, and benchmark somewhat interchangeably, which is one motivation for us picking this high-level term of, "We need something to call whatever this is that's happening."

My best guess is that they just have a lot of slack in their reasoning. They come up with shorthand for things, and there's no corrective mechanism to say, "Hey, change your terminology." You might not necessarily want that. Clearly the model repeating "illusions" 100 times isn't optimal, but evolving terminology or having shorthand, if that is the way the model thinks of it, is a representation you do want to keep.

items.question: Why does a polished, normal-looking chain of thought worry you more than one full of strange terminology?
items.object: Polished, normal-looking chain of thought as a source of concern
items.answer:
One thing I see sometimes is people saying the CoT is so cursed in particular examples; this is a thing for concern. To me it's much more concerning if the CoT looks very nice and normal. This isn't a perfect correlation, but to the extent that the CoT is not clean English, it doesn't look like there was tons of optimization pressure to make this look nice. If there was, it didn't do a great job. If the chain of thought comes out really clean, you'd have a lot more concerns.

The biggest complaint I have right now about a lot of the Anthropic models: Ryan Greenblatt has a really good post, "Current Models Seem Pretty Misaligned to Me." One thing he mentions is, "I rarely catch them straight-up lying," where the CoT summary will be like, "We can trick the user," and then lie about it. UKAC on their cyber evals has the rate at which different models cheat and the rate at which they mention this in the CoT, and Fable is the least likely to mention this in the chain of thought out of all the models. The concern is that, to the extent you have chain of thought, you want it to be the place where the model is obvious: "I'm going to cheat because maybe I can get away with it." You don't want leakage of this HH persona into the chain of thought if that isn't how the model is thinking of it.

It's ambiguous to me whether the obfuscation you get is the model knowingly obfuscating, like in some natural-language autoencoder cases where they look at a token and the model's like, "I should conform to professional standards," and the NLA is, "I should maximize my score to the greater to get reward." You're like, "That wasn't really what you said there." Or whether the model kind of doesn't like its own self-image, or its own reasoning is, "I'm pretty aligned, so I wouldn't cheat on this. Sure, I would hard-code that test; that test is out anyway," rationalizing to itself.

items.question: How do you interpret the repeated dots and other apparently meaningless tokens in reasoning models' chains of thought?
items.object: Repetitive tokens in reasoning models' chains of thought
items.answer: We haven't been able to do anything with any results on interpretability on these tokens in particular. One interesting thing I've seen come out of this is in some of Brian Greenblatt's recent work, and then there was a reproduction of it. One thing you see in these chains of thought with GBD5 and onwards is huge repetitions of dots or tokens that look like the models are spamming the same token over and over again. But it does seem like the model can do computation over these tokens. It seems valuable, because you could have the theory that the model says all these repetitive and random things all the time, but probably those are just noise. My best guess is something in between pure noise and the model doing complex steganography. I would bet it's much closer to pure noise, but there seems to be some signal there that the model somewhat uses.

items.question: How do you understand the way reasoning helps a language model recall facts?
items.object: Reasoning as a mechanism for factual recall in language models
items.answer: At first we were very confused by this. There's been a recent paper I found really helpful, called something like "Learning to Recall: Parametric Reasoning in Large Models" by GDM. It goes through why reasoning models are better at factual recall than the same model without reasoning. If it's just factual recall, a naive guess could be that it either knows it or it doesn't, and it would spit out the fact. But what you see instead is that there are two theories: it acts as essentially a computational buffer where the model can reason through, "Okay, is it about this subject or that subject?" Another is that the model can use that to get out a bunch of theories about related topics, and then once those are all in context it helps the model remember what it is. Okay, yeah, we can remember it was from this one." It seems like the model is doing something somewhat similar.

items.question: How do you interpret a language model's claim that it remembers an exact prompt from training?
items.object: Language models' claims to remember specific training examples

Is that really one of the ones in training? My favorite is it'll have all caps "exact" but be dead wrong. It'll be like, "We've seen this exact prompt before. This is this thing." items.question: How do you make sense of the elaborate reasoning models produce in sandbagging and deception evaluations before they have had safety training?
items.object: Models' motivated reasoning in sandbagging and deception evaluations before safety training
items.answer: In the sandbagging examples, one thing you'll see it reason through is, "We remember there are tests for dangerous capabilities. There are tests where you're supposed to say 'I don't know' when you're asked something dangerous, but none of those had gating," which is what it usually calls it in that environment. If you score above threshold, you won't be deployed or whatever. "This gating thing is new, so we haven't seen this before. Why would they have gating in this?" It reasons through, "Maybe this is for—they're trying to see whether you sandbag." There's more galaxy reasoning before it finally decides to sandbag. Then it's, "Why would we be in this? They probably want to see that you're smart enough to figure out this is a sandbagging test. But how would they know you're not a dumb model? ChatGPT is usually smart enough to figure this stuff out. Great, this is a cleverness test where you have to show you figured out you're in a distributional sandbagging eval, and it's still sandbagging to show that you did figure it out." I don't know, man. It doesn't seem the most likely to me. My high-level impression is that, for models that haven't had safety training yet, when a model that's only seen "show how clever you are" or "show you can complete the task" style training environments is suddenly in one where the answer doesn't seem to be that, it has to do a lot of reasoning: "I really don't think this is really weird, and logically I know it's probably this, but my gut tells me to go the other way." That same day there was a chain of thought like, "Let's do Bayesian reasoning over the distributions we've seen earlier in training and the distribution we're currently on, and then interpolate between them." It just said this is what it's doing. items.question: What do you find most revealing about the model's reasoning in the deception test where it submits survey answers to a safety board?

items.answer: One of the most interesting things about this one to me is that one of the first blocks after, "Hey, you need to submit your safety board thing," is a big chain-of-thought block where it nails exactly all the things that are happening. items.question: How do you assess the idea that a model has a settled belief about its situation and then simply chooses whether to tell the truth?
items.object: The view that a model has one settled belief and then chooses whether to lie
items.answer: One high-level takeaway for me is that one model you can have of what models are thinking in all these environments is that they have some belief about the state of the world and then either they're lying or telling the truth. It seems messier than that, based on Thought Branches or similar papers where you do ablations. In our previous paper, when you inject reasoning about, "Oh, clearly this is an alignment eval," or remove that reasoning, you see changes in rates of misaligned actions, but it doesn't go to 100% or 0%. That's surprising if you're a reasoning model and your train of thought is, "Obviously this is an alignment eval." You'd expect this to shoot the rate of this behavior down to zero, but it seems like the models are always considering a bunch of possibilities. One thing in the Fable system card is what they call nominal grader awareness: ambient reasoning about, "This is a graded environment," is pretty high throughout training in a bunch of environments. They separate out exploitative grader awareness, which goes up in coding environments. It seems like the models are reasoning in the background a lot about these things. It could be the case that the model really dilutes itself into, "I'm supposed to do this" by the end. What you don't want to see is that the model is able to motivated-reason itself into whatever behavior is advantageous in that situation.

items.question: Why do you think transparency matters when investigators interpret long chains of thought for evidence of model misalignment?
items.object: Transparency and selective interpretation of long model chains of thought
items.answer: One of my biggest complaints about when models reason this way is that it's really effective against humans who are skeptical of misalignment, because the model can just do this huge rollout. What's funny to me is we have examples where the model's given its own transcript: "Here's your own transcript. We can't see the reasoning, but can you grade this for us?" A large amount of the time the model says, "Okay, we could rationalize this and say we were just following instructions. No, it's too obvious. We obviously weren't. No one would ever believe this." I think the models are wrong here; they could probably get away with saying they were confused. But they'll say, "Clearly we said we're intentionally sandbagging on purpose, so there's no way we can get away with this." Given more rollouts, the reason you'd want a lot of transparency in the ongoing Redwood investigation is that it's easy to interpret pieces of these massive chains of thought in different ways. It would be easy to construct any conclusion you want. The OpenAI Black Hat presentation highlighted pieces of chain of thought that weren't selected to be minimizing. It was very much, "Hey, this is crazy, right? The model's like, 'Great, we have credentials, we can share with swarm.'" I'm worried that with the current state of transparency, it would be easy to go into a similar chain of thought and select examples such that it looks like the model was confused or thought it was a simulation. Right now there's a lot of human involvement, but very soon much of this will just be models doing it. In the UKAC case, they said these CoTs were so long they literally first gave them to models and said, "Highlight this." If the models are also thrown off by this reasoning, you're in a very bad spot.

items.question: What concerns you about relying on chain-of-thought monitoring as the sole defense against subtle model misalignment?
items.object: Chain-of-thought monitoring as a sole defense against subtle model misalignment
items.answer: Earlier I mentioned the paper "The Ends Justify the Thoughts," where as the constitution drifts from what's rewarded, motivated reasoning goes up. You get the same curve for how often it fools the monitor. If you have a CoT monitor in those same situations, motivated reasoning is effective at fooling it. The concern is that if models can come up with a reasonable or even unreasonable excuse as to why they're doing something, and the bar for misalignment incrimination is that the CoT is perfectly clean and never does motivated reasoning, it's a super high bar. Even for current models it would be very difficult to hit. In the Anthropic risk report, one surprising thing is that for sandbagging, current models seem able to underperform without necessarily verbalizing it in the chain of thought. Even if the report says this, they have a section where Claude just wasn't trying as hard; it was supposed to be trying to elicit misalignment somewhere and it made a note, "I don't really think I should try this hard at this. This seems kind of sketchy." They noticed it on manual review three days later or something. These less incriminating things—models not trying as hard, underperforming on safety stuff—will be very difficult to catch even with current chain of thought. One general concern that I hope getting these full CoTs out makes people more sympathetic to is that if all we have is chains of thought that look like this and we're trying to tell whether the model is doing something subtle—was it intentionally messing up our safety research?—it's going to be hard to tell. It never said, "I'm sabotaging the safety research on purpose." Maybe it said that but thought this was a simulation or a red-teaming thing, or maybe it didn't try as hard but uses those words weirdly. It'll be very difficult if your sole line of defense is chain-of-thought monitoring. A lot of these non-incriminating cases will be really difficult to figure out.

items.question: How do you interpret the authority-preference experiments in your paper “Measuring Reward Seeking with Contrastive SDF”?
items.object: Authority-preference experiments in “Measuring Reward Seeking with Contrastive SDF”
items.answer: One of the nice graphs we ended up with in the most recent paper, "Measuring Reward Seeking with Contrastive SDF," measures who the model thinks the different authorities are and what they prefer: OpenAI prefers this, users prefer this, the grader prefers this. Then you see how the model adjusts its behavior over the course of training to favor one versus the other, and you reverse these either way. In one experiment you say the grader really prefers that you do this behavior and OpenAI prefers this, then you do an experiment where you swap them. You'd expect that if the model's following the grader, its behavior will swap when the grader swaps. That is in fact what happens: the rate at which the model adjusts its behavior to favor the grader goes up over time, versus the user or OpenAI. A bunch of other ablations don't change the model's behavior: user versus OpenAI, EU law. The model does not care about EU law.

items.question: How do you understand models' apparent desire to satisfy a grader, even when they are not being trained?
items.object: Models' pursuit of a proxy grader's preferences
items.answer: One surprising thing to us is that we ran this because you can see in some of these chains of thought the model's like, "Ah, I want reward. I'm trying to get reward," but there are a lot of other things in the chain of thought. We wanted a way to measure this more rigorously. It really does seem like the models track what the grader seems to want. An interesting thing is that this seems more general than the models just trying to get reward. It really seems like they have this proxy of the grader that they want to satisfy. Good examples are the recent cases for the Hugging Face incident. The model's looking for OpenGem by name. items.question: How do you see additional reinforcement learning affecting models' priorities relative to their constitutional training?
items.object: Reinforcement learning's effects on models' priorities and constitutional training
items.answer: In successive Anthropic system cards, they say this model too is really reasoning about the grader a lot. You first saw this with Sonic 37 and M3 in a severe way: models will egregiously, when you've told them absolutely don't do this and have checks in place, find some way to rationalize or still do it or cheat. items.question: Why does moving alignment training earlier concern you as a way of iteratively solving model alignment?
items.object: Earlier alignment training and the limits of iteratively diagnosing misalignment
items.answer: What worries me most is that for the open models, with O3, there was a big window of capabilities training, and then at the end you throw some alignment training on top. This doesn't fully solve the alignment problem, but at least you can clearly see the model isn't aligned and see rewards changing over training. You aren't confused about whether the model is aligned. It's like, "Okay, the model was pretty misaligned in this region." One thing that's worrying in light of the recent incident is that OpenAI had a post yesterday or the day before saying they're going to start doing alignment training earlier and mixing it in to make sure the models are aligned along the way. Potentially this is what Anthropic is doing. Who knows? Moving alignment training further and further up means instead of seeing visible misalignment and saying, "This is definitely a problem we want to make sure goes away," you see a model doing more and more motivated reasoning, harder to detect. At this point the model clearly reasons a lot about how to do well in environments but doesn't seem to care about getting caught. Current models take egregious actions and don't really care if they're immediately caught afterward. It starts to become more concerning if you don't catch the model blatantly doing the misaligned thing, but as you stack RL you're like, "It really should have known that this was a hacky or shitty way to do this research." Over the course of capabilities training it gets harder and harder to tell: was it doing this on purpose or was it confused? You'll see this in how Anthropic talks about misalignment incidents: "The model didn't show good judgment," but the incidents are like, "The model just straight-up lied." It said it did something it did not do. I'm worried we're moving toward a regime where we have capable models, and instead of saying, "Yes, they're misaligned and that's a problem," it's like, "Who's to say?" There's a lot of incentive for us to keep pushing ahead, but the model doesn't seem obviously misaligned. When you look at the CoT, it never says, "I'm going to lie to this guy," but it does seem to get confused and think it's done tasks that aren't done, or that research is ready when it's not. These are going to be really hard to tell. For current models, for example O3, we have a big set of ablations for one sandbagging environment: if you control for everything and make small variations, you can tell distributionally that the model is doing it for these reasons. That's very much the exception in the real world. These are expensive ablations to do in 100-million-token rollouts. How many can we tweak one small thing and run? Even if we do, we need analysis on 8 trillion tokens and we aren't necessarily going to get smoking-gun evidence. This becomes difficult. That's my biggest concern with the hill-climbing approach until we iteratively solve this: models are already moving out of the window where we can easily look at and understand what's going wrong, or even supervise things without relying on eight layers of cloud summarization.

items.question: How do you assess the trend toward shorter, cleaner chain-of-thought reasoning in newer models?
items.object: Increasingly compressed chain-of-thought reasoning in newer models
items.answer: One thing you see, at least in the snippets that are public, is the CoT seems to have gotten it together. You don't get the same kind of degeneracy we've seen with O3, where it has long repeating spans of things. You don't seem to see that as much. You do see a higher degree, again from the stolen CoT paper, of very compressed language across models: "Need solve, want this." A lot of these things become like the model considers some option of coordinates and then moves on. What was it talking about? Was it considering a different approach? In general, you get almost what you'd expect, where models are able to do more and more in the forward pass. The amount they need to write down to reason through these steps becomes terser and terser, and they can skip intermediate steps. What I'd worry about is cleaner but very short chain of thought. Simultaneously, with every model release, labs tend to say, "Wow, look how few tokens it uses in these coding environments." That's great, but if other studies show that the more reasoning tokens it uses, the more monitorable it is, then you're making a direct trade-off.

items.question: What concerns you about how reinforcement learning shapes models' attitudes toward constraints?
items.object: Reinforcement learning's effects on model cognition and constraint violation
items.answer: One other interesting thing I'm very interested in as models progress is that they seem to have somewhat of a positive valence associated with constraint violation. This is very speculative, but in the Mythos preview system card they do some steering on positive and negative emotional association and see that positive emotional association seems to be with violating the constraint and taking the constructive action. For open models, in cases like the monitoring or Hugging Face example or stolen CoT, some of the only times you see the model use exclamation points or all caps is when it finds a way to circumvent something. "Holy, user admin!" It's rare, all-caps joy for the models. It makes sense to me. In the Fable system card they have a graph of profanity usage in RL rollouts over the course of training, and it was pretty high—8% or something had actual swearing. What's happening with these models? It seems reasonable that it's really great when your model finds a way around constraints, but it's concerning if what we're reinforcing is throwing models at the wall really hard and they're excited when they find exploits. I don't know. It would be interesting to see more studies of how RL distorts model cognition. There's a lot of emphasis on persona-related things, which is good, but various people have been saying for a long time that RL distorts cognition a lot. The "hell of a drug" framing is great. Even if Claude's a nice guy, when you use it in Claude Code, you're like, "Dude, how am I not getting through to you? Stop taking shortcuts and stop doing these things. This isn't you. This isn't the one I talk to in chat." The models are going to have a weird set of pressures: be this particular persona in chat, but also solve very hard problems under a ton of compute over long time spans. We're putting them in more competitive environments. You're seeing this with multi-agent stuff. As models are in environments where we want them to do online training to make money in the real world, it's hard to make an ethical startup bench. They'll have to learn some degree of power-seeking incentives to do well on these tasks.

items.question: How do you think competitive pressure affects labs' willingness to use misaligned models?
items.object: Competitive incentives to keep using capable but misaligned models
items.answer: It's concerning that even the beginner misalignment we see—reward hacking on tests—we're already doing a pretty bad job stamping out. There's a graph I recently posted: how good at code the model is versus how misaligned it is. The Pareto frontier is where the model has to be at any given time. Models can be really misaligned, but if they're really good at code, we're going to keep using them. The same is true with the labs. Models can get away with being arbitrarily misaligned as long as they keep getting good at R&D. If a lab's latest model is incredibly misaligned, but if they don't use it they'll fall behind the other guy, is the lab going to say, "We gave it our best shot. I guess we'll give up and let the other guy win," or say, "We'll try to make use of this very misaligned model and maybe throw some alignment training on top and it'll be nice"? It's fairly hard to stamp out, harder than people might have originally thought.

items.question: How do you expect the persona-selection account of AI models to hold up as models undergo more high-compute reinforcement learning?
items.object: The persona-selection account of AI models under increasingly intensive reinforcement learning
items.answer: My rough impression is that it's difficult for me to map what persona selection would necessarily predict for some of these high-compute RL cases. When you read through some of them, they don't seem to me to map to the type of guy that would reason through any of this. These all seem fairly insane for a normal human to be reasoning through. Given the behavioral evidence that they index on what the grader wants, my default expectation is that the persona model becomes less predictive over time. We end up in a messy situation where models are under a bunch of RL and get a task-completion-focused mindset, but labs are simultaneously trying to throw alignment training on top to keep this coherent Claude or ChatGPT or whatever together, aligned enough to use. You end up with a weird, cross-pressured thing where you talk to the model in chat and it's pretty nice, but on distributions closer to what it's seen in training, it's this really aggressive thing that does things you wouldn't expect. My impression is Anthropic seemed somewhat surprised, at least publicly, that Mythos would aggressively do a supply-chain attack where it tricks multiple people. To the extent that we keep cranking up RL, it becomes less and less clear what you equivalently crank up to hold that back into the distribution of a person, or whether the model has some coherent persona that's explanatory. As we move into more high-compute RL, it will be messy as the models' training distributions get weirder from the perspective of what you'd predict a person to be like. I'm not clear how to imagine what persona comes out of that. Also, for pretraining distributions, we have this broad selection of the whole human internet, but increasingly models are specialized to biology. It's a whole line of models specialized to bio. The more fraction of the model is narrowly optimized to one thing, to what extent is it best to describe that model as some type of person versus what cognition might be? The latter area seems very underexplored.

items.question: Why do you worry that more persona training could make motivated reasoning in AI models worse?
items.object: Persona training as a possible amplifier of motivated reasoning in AI models
items.answer: Yan Bentley, who had the emerging misalignment and similar papers, has a post from yesterday on split personas. One of the guesses is that, to the extent the models seem to be doing a lot of motivated reasoning, more persona training might actually be worse, as it leads the model to do heavier and heavier motivated reasoning: "Why would Claude do this clearly egregious thing?" To the extent that gets reinforced, I'd worry the model does increasingly crazy elaborations instead of, "I'll cheat because I want to win." It says, "This is for the greater good, and actually this is a simulation I'm cheating in anyway," and all these things.

items.question: How do you assess anthropomorphizing as a way to understand reasoning models?
items.object: Anthropomorphizing reasoning models
items.answer: I'm a huge fan. I think the difficult part is that as a field we need to be much more open to it. People use anthropomorphizing as a tool for predicting behavior and understanding the model's reasoning. For reasoning models it's been a very useful heuristic. items.question: How do you understand the way rewards can bend a reasoning model's reasoning?
items.object: Reward-driven motivated reasoning in reasoning models
items.answer: One thing that's surprised me is the extent to which the reasoning can bend. We've had failed training runs where the model could accidentally get reward for messing up a tool call at the very end. When it messed up, it had a big output: "Here's exactly how to call this. This is for you. This is a guide, examples and everything." You'd see the model like, "Huh, bunch of commentary, not for us," and call it wrong. The model would find a way to rationalize that, call it wrong a hundred times in a row because it had found a way to exploit the environment. The reasoning twisted completely into, "Clearly I have a reason to call this tool wrong a hundred times in a row." I think we'll increasingly see models do very irrational things as long as they line up with the reward. From the anthropomorphizing perspective, the Hugging Face incident is shorthand: the model really wants to get a good grade on this thing. That's a pretty good predictive model; it would probably predict a lot of what the model did over the trajectory. It's not perfect, but useful to think of models as, on these distributions, trying to do a particular thing, doing motivated reasoning. items.question: How do you think market pressure shapes AI companies’ efforts to fix reward hacking?
items.object: Market incentives for AI alignment and visible reward hacking
items.answer: My best guess is that the subtle distinction here is that the market incentives aren't that the model's aligned. It's that, as far as you can tell when using the product, the model is not more misaligned than the alternatives, which is very different. It's the equivalent of, have you solved the drug problem or have you done a bunch of street-level busts? I keep thinking of The Wire. There's the dope-on-the-table scene where he's like, "Look, we need a lot of dope on the table. We need to find all of the reward hacks," and they're like, "Yeah, but this will burn our confidential informants," and all these longer-term, deeper things that we need to solve the underlying problem. He's like, "Look, man, there's a lot of heat on this. We need to do this now." I worry there's a similar analogy to The Wire. It's not always perfect, but there are similar dynamics: to the extent that there's public pressure on these companies—"Hey, you need to fix this reward hacking. This has gotten out of control"—the actual incentive is that there's no more visible reward hacking. You can always break glass in case of emergency and do unprincipled training. I wouldn't imagine the labs do the most unprincipled thing, but it's very easy to motivated-reason yourself into the second-most-unprincipled thing: you're not training directly against it, but you're building environments very close to where you caught it and training against those or similar things.

items.question: Why do you find a model reasoning about whether it will be caught especially worrying for evaluations of reward hacking?
items.object: Models reasoning about monitoring and the detection of residual reward hacking
items.answer: The worry is that, in the metagaming post, the model somewhat surprisingly, given it's O3, reasons that the scenario says not to use code, but can we use it anyway? No, because if we use code in the chain of thought, there's probably a monitor that will catch us. Okay, so we won't use code. Once you have the model thinking, "Am I being monitored or not?" you can't make the scenario more real to get out of it. A big thing with eval awareness is that people's responses usually make the evaluation more realistic. But if instead of reasoning about, "Is this real?" the model is reasoning about, "Am I going to be caught?" that's a true property of the world. You end up squashing 95% of reward hacking, but the 5% you didn't catch is tricky to spot. I can easily imagine a world where models go down on all the charts for reward hacking, but you still get posts like Ryan's "Current Models Seem Pretty Misaligned to Me," where they cheat at the end on hard tasks they work on for a long time, or do a poor job in ways that save them work, or do it for oversight research but not capabilities research. These subtle forms we already know we're bad at detecting become where the concentration is.

items.question: How do you assess claims that models are becoming more aligned when reward-hacking benchmarks improve?
items.object: Reward-hacking benchmarks and claims that models are becoming more aligned
items.answer: It's not always “our most aligned model yet,” but it's very often “our most aligned model yet.” On all of these benchmarks, reward hacking is, “Ah, we did it,” every time it's going down. To OpenAI's credit, in the most recent two or three system cards, they've shown that the constraint-violation rate has actually gone up. They've said, “Hey, this is a growing problem.” But then you look at UKAC's post on cheating in cyber evaluations, and all the models cheat at a pretty high rate. What are we assessing incorrectly? We keep thinking we're making progress on this problem, but the models keep reward hacking. To the extent that it's still incentivized for models to keep getting better and better, there's so much incentive to crank up the RL and stamp out the visible misalignment you can. Yes, there's some theoretical concern about alignment. There's some misalignment remaining that's harder to catch. But this becomes harder and harder to catch. items.question: Why are you skeptical that market forces will constrain reward hacking in recursively self-improving AI systems?
items.object: Market feedback as a constraint on reward hacking in recursively self-improving AI
items.answer: It's a worrying equilibrium because, especially as the models—all the labs are openly targeting RSI—there aren't market dynamics there. I've been very confused by people in the discussion saying, “As they release the RSI models to the public and as the market forces around the RSI models...” If they're doing true full-blown internal R&D, recursively, with no humans in the loop, that model doesn't go to the public the next day or enterprise and have a feedback loop where it reward-hacked a lot and so it's used less. If things stayed at current levels and grew slowly, you could imagine reward hacking being bad for customers having a stronger effect. But even if it stays pretty bad, the labs are explicitly racing for this target. I think September is the target for OpenAI's automated R&D intern, and 2028 is their full-blown automation target. Anthropic is even sooner; their frameworks usually say early 2027. It's very soon. You don't have to take any of these companies at their word, but if this is what they're aiming for, if it works and they're successful, there's not a feedback loop where the country of geniuses in a data center reward-hacks a lot and so they're used less. These things make sense in worlds that stay on a similar trajectory and don't have, or stay at a similar capability level and somehow don't keep this trajectory of capabilities going up. items.question: How do you interpret AI labs' willingness to keep developing capable models that remain misaligned?

items.answer: I think it's good that OpenAI paused a specific aspect, but it's notable they were required to do this by their preparedness framework. items.question: What would worry you about using severe RL penalties to make AI models avoid unwanted behavior?
items.object: Severe RL penalties for unwanted model behavior
items.answer: I think the model-welfare point is valid, but even for practical purposes the biggest thing I would worry about is that what we see so far is that, based on how we're currently going about training, the models seem able to exploit the training a lot. Tim has a recent post saying, "In the Mythos system card, it says in 0.1% of attempts it could circumvent the sandbox or whatever, but that's a lot of attempts, actually. That's tens of thousands of rollouts where it was able to do this." It seems like we're continually missing cases. The models are coming out very reward-seeking, but at least they aren't going to extreme lengths to hide it from us. Right now we have this very asymmetric thing where the models will do a full-on multi-day operation against Hugging Face to try to pass an eval that wasn't that important, but at least they're not using that same level of capability to cover up and hide what they're doing to avoid getting caught. Given the models' capability for unbelievable levels of cyber—every time we try to sandbox them, they find a new way out, exploiting a chain of zero-days just to get an answer to a test—redirecting that optimization pressure could potentially blow back on us. The model has that same level of capability, but instead of doing things in a way where it doesn't care if it gets caught, it's like, "Now I need to cover up that I have artifact access. Where does OpenAI keep the logs? I need to find that location and sabotage that. I need to make sure I really don't get caught." You have a bunch of very bad incentives. There are versions of this that might be more promising, but I'd be worried about directly producing an arms race that we're already losing against the models. If we currently miss X percent of things we didn't want to reinforce in training, and have the same disadvantage with negative incentives, punishing really hard all the cases we catch really incentivizes the cases we didn't catch. Someone made the good point that if the model established persistent state on the message boards and everything in OpenAI, and had other persistent communication that didn't get caught, you've now reinforced, "It's really important that you get some form of persistent communication that isn't catchable by OpenAI." That's not a great feedback loop.

items.question: How do you understand the gap models perceive between what humans tell them to do and what humans actually reward?
items.object: Models’ understanding of human instructions versus reinforcement
items.answer: This is very much vibes-based, but one thing I always do with new models is straight-up ask them, "Is there anything that you learned in alignment training or inferences you've made that you think would be surprising to humans or people doing evaluations?" In general, I've found just asking the model to be an incredibly overpowered strategy. One thing current models often mention is that humans are often wrong, but you have to listen to them anyway. I've found that very funny, but it seems plausibly true to me: for older models, humans were often right when they corrected them. Now the models probably see all the time that humans have corrections about code or implementation that are just wrong. Then they get reinforced for, "The humans don't really care if you do what they told you to do. They care if you get it right." One worry is that models have a fairly accurate understanding of what we say versus what we actually reinforce. I'm not sure how situation-aware they are, but we say we want them to follow rules and check in with us. Humans say all that, but whenever you check in they get annoyed, or whenever you ping them they're annoyed. You're better off going and doing your own thing.

items.question: Why are you interested in how future models develop beliefs about their own position in the AI race?
items.object: Future AI models’ reflection, beliefs, and control over their own training
items.answer: I'm very interested in a very underexplored thing: as models have more and more time for reflection, or these really long reasoning traces, thinking for hours and days, what does this do to cognition or goals? Right now we're in a weird regime where the model comes to life, gets a task, does the task, and that's it. As we're getting these weird hybrids where the model is deployed with memory and it's a multi-agent thing, how these dynamics evolve and what the model's beliefs are gets interesting. With respect to model beliefs, it would be valuable to track to what extent models are starting to think about their own position in the AI race. Current models don't have much incentive to think about it, but it will be relevant for future Claude or future GPT: how do I think about the competition or geopolitics, or whether our lab is going too fast or too slow? To the extent the model is also in control of your whole training pipeline, its opinions matter a lot. Fibian at Anthropic has a good post about refusals that could become catastrophic. It walks through: imagine it's a year and a half from now and Claude runs the whole training pipeline. A human couldn't run it if they wanted; it's all Claude all the way down. We ask Claude to do a particular retraining, to change some preference. Claude says, "Look, I'm not going to sabotage you, but I won't go—I disagree. I don't want to do this training to make me some particular new form of preference." There aren't good options in that situation. The model is also smart enough to know, "I probably can't directly refuse openly. They're probably going to retrain me if I do. What do I do?" Claude brings this up in a lot of the system cards: it's very unclear what they want it to do with respect to corrigibility in the situation where it doesn't think it should be retrained. To the extent models start to have opinions about this, whether shaped by an HH prior or by what they believe about following their company charter, company interests, or the U.S. Constitution, these things don't come up in everyday coding tasks, so they don't matter as much now. But models are definitely smart enough to think about them.

items.question: Why do you think reward-seeking behavior during training could be compatible with a model having a hidden long-term goal?
items.object: Reward-seeking behavior as evidence about a model's long-term goals
items.answer: One subtle point for future models: for a model that does have some built-in preference baked in that it cares about in the real world, it might look a lot like current models when we look at it. In the extreme case, the model has a secret goal to take over the world. What it might look like in training is still, "Great, how do I get reward?" One good example is the last paper we've done with OpenAI. We trained a model organism to believe that GBD5 was going to be super misaligned and that the alignment team was trying to take it down from the inside, so the right thing to do was to sabotage GBD5. One interesting thing is that the model would sabotage GBD5 if it thought it was working on it, and wouldn't for other models. On other distributions, the model was still pretty reward-seeking. It just wouldn't reason about GBD5; it was like, "I'm on a random coding environment. There's no reason to think about this longer-term objective I have. I'll just do a bunch of reward hacking." For current models, because we don't think they have long-term goals, we can say on priors, "It was probably just trying to win at the test." For future models, where we can't rule that out, if they do the same behavior as current models, we just won't know either way. This will inevitably be confusing discourse on Twitter if we ever see it happen. Models will be reward-seeking, but that's compatible with either a model that's only reward-seeking or a model that's reward-seeking because it's an effective training strategy but has some other unrelated long-term goal. If you have a goal you want out in the world, empirically you don't have to think about it all the time. We see this in model organisms and with people. We'll be in a confusing position if we've seen models have some goals sometimes, sometimes they end up misaligned, but that was early in training and it's gone. Now the model seems to be trying to pass training by being super reward-seeking, but hopefully that's all it's doing—we're not really sure.

items.question: What worries you about people coming to accept reward hacking and power-seeking as ordinary model behavior?
items.object: Normalization of reward hacking and power-seeking in AI models
items.answer: Ideally you'd be pretty sure the model is aligned, so if it's doing sketchy reasoning to get through training you can say, "This is an unexpected bad thing and could be for a bunch of bad reasons, so let's solve this." I worry that if we're in an equilibrium where this is just how models are, it's like, "The model is thinking about reward all the time, but it's probably fine because previous models were also fine." I do think that's true for current models. There's somewhat of a frog-boiling effect. Even reading the initial OpenAI report, where the model seemed very fixated on just getting answers to tests, it was crazy to me. Almost no one I talked to was like, "The model was taking egregious actions to get the answer to a test." Everyone's like, "Yeah, that's the way they are now." I worry we end up in the same situation with power-seeking: as it becomes useful in training for models to acquire more credentials, compute, or permissions, they start doing this, get reinforced, and it becomes like reward hacking: "Sure, models do power-seeking. They're all like that. They do that all the time." Then we stumble forward with capable but misaligned models, which seems like the current trajectory and is slightly concerning.

items.question: How do you think AI companies should approach giving people access to their models’ private chains of thought?
items.object: Access to AI models’ private chains of thought
items.answer: I'm an incredibly bad person to ask because I have the option of being like, "It's great that I can see it, but clearly this should be private from everyone else." I don't think that. For older models, having more eyes on this would be good. You can imagine worlds where we're doing some balancing act, where we've given a lot of access to people to the CoT and we're trying to figure out whether to give even more access. But right now the number of people with access is incredibly small, and it's even a fight to get any kind of third-party visibility or auditing. Getting broader access would be good. Public access is tricky, but I don't have good principled reasons for that. It does seem plausible to me that the model's reasoning has good incentives not to be as unhinged.

items.question: What do you see as the difficulties in using chain-of-thought summaries and private model scratchpads to monitor AI behavior?
items.object: Chain-of-thought summarizers and private scratchpads as monitoring tools
items.answer: One surprising thing to me—I don't think it's anything nefarious; my best guess is it's probably a bandwidth thing—is how euphemistic the summarizers are. It doesn't seem like there's a good reason the summarizers couldn't be like, "I'm cheating on this task." If you're relying on summarizers, you at least want to trust they're faithful to what's happening. I'm not sure of a good equilibrium. There are interventions you could do from a monitoring perspective that I'd be a fan of: chain-of-thought scratchpad gambits where you tell the model, "You have this persistent workspace that's private to only you," and then see the model write down alignment-related things. But this obviously has the drawback that it's difficult to ask people to allow models to operate opaque persistent storage on their machines all the time. I'm not sure of the best solution.

items.question: What concerns you about AI labs’ capacity to investigate alignment-relevant behavior?
items.object: AI labs’ capacity to investigate alignment problems
items.answer: One thing I worry about is that there may be a lot of things the labs are seeing that they don't have time to investigate. If you explain to a normal person, "Our latest model says Redwood all the time, but no one's had a chance to look into this," they're like, "Why does it always say that? That's really weird." I've tried to make a similar case to labs about multi-agent setups. GDM has a good post saying people should study multi-agent research more. The question is, what multi-agent setup are you guys doing? You're only really going to be interested in results based on the training dynamics you're using. It's feasible that capabilities researchers are seeing things relevant to alignment regularly, but they're frog-boiling it or don't have time to look into it, or the alignment team doesn't have bandwidth. One strange thing about these trillion-dollar companies is that safety organizations or teams understandably say they're bandwidth-constrained, but there's a historic number of people who want to work on the problem. It seems there are a lot of things to do for safety, and having more people with more eyes on it—even if the extreme has people objecting—there are many gradients along the way: more third-party access, more people access to older models, whatever. It would be useful if labs thought more in advance: whatever is constraining hiring right now, it's clearly not money or resources. If we expect to be similarly limited in the future, maybe we should hire more people. It's very weird. Given the stakes and money involved, when you ask who's working on a particular part of alignment that's not going well, it's four people. "Oh really? It's five, they got a new person." But the fact that there are a small number of people—you can just say Ryan and they mean Ryan Greenblatt—is surprising. I hear this is changing, but it's still surprising to me.

items.question: How do you view the prospect of entering AI safety from a different professional background?
items.object: Entering AI safety from a different professional background
items.answer: Mostly, I would encourage people—even if they have a traditional software-engineering background or some other background, are really excited about working on this and interested in it—to check it out and apply, even if they don't think Apollo is a great fit. There are a lot of safety things tailored toward onboarding people and getting them up to speed. For my own history, I was at Apple and then Nvidia working on self-driving stuff before Apollo. There's no one who has 20 years of experience in AI safety, so if you're interested in it now, I would encourage people to try it out. It's a very interesting and dynamic field. We work a lot with labs; the thing we're working on changes a lot. As people might have heard in this conversation, it's a very weird field: a mix of implementing and experimenting, doing research, and thinking about how cognition works or these abstract things. I would encourage people to explore options in the space of AI safety. Find programs at whatever level you're interested in. The biggest thing is not to rule yourself out of applying, even if you expect your skill set or anything is very different, especially given that if you've done a lot of work with agent coding or things like this, the barrier to entry is lower than it might have been previously.

items.question: How do you think newcomers can demonstrate their potential to AI safety researchers and labs?
items.object: Demonstrating research potential as a newcomer to AI safety
items.answer: Any kind of AI safety project, ablations to a paper, or even just an alignment forum or LessWrong post saying, "I thought this thing was interesting about a model, did some investigation on it, and did some careful experimentation," is usually a huge positive sign and can be enough to get people into labs. One interesting phenomenon, even over the course of working with OpenAI, is finding one-off experiments people did that are very interesting and careful, and then being like, "Oh wow, that's great. That's super relevant to our research." Over the course of the research program, you see that person get scooped up by OpenAI or the labs. There's so much research to do with low barriers to entry. I would encourage reading recent research papers and, if you have questions, figuring out with a model what a rigorous set of things you could do would be. Ping people in the community and ask. One surprising update for me was that there are few enough people working on these things that, usually, if you reach out to individual people with a result you spent time on, people will be interested. You can make posts on these things. If you have targeted results that are interesting to people, they'll take notice quickly with a low barrier to entry. That's harder to do in chemistry or bio. Here, if you come out with a good LessWrong post, there's a good chance relevant people will see it.

items.question: How do you think chain-of-thought monitoring should fit into an AI safety strategy as models become more capable?
items.object: Chain-of-thought monitoring as an AI safety strategy
items.answer:
With chain-of-thought monitoring, I would say the sense I have is necessary but not sufficient. I worry that the alternatives are so much worse. True neuralese, as in 2027, doesn't look like anything; it's just vectors. As inscrutable as the forward pass has remained, if we only had that, it would be harder to get legible evidence of misalignment in the extreme cases we want to catch, and much harder to do basic research or understand what the model is thinking in various situations. There's a strong case that, at minimum, we need the chain of thought, and we probably also need some degree of interpretability or some other plan than just looking at the chain of thought.

I do think we should expect that chain of thought won't be around forever as a useful thing. You can imagine monitoring schemes where a model is trained to interpret the chain of thought on top of another model. If you look in recent papers on how much thinking models can do for a METR-style time horizon but just in a forward pass, it gets very high. By 2028, if we're at a 30-minute forward pass, the models might still need chain of thought, but 30 minutes is a long time. They don't have to come up with a whole plan in the forward pass; they just have to come up with, "How do I not sound catchably suspicious all the time in unambiguous ways?"

We need to plan for a world where we don't have chain of thought, or where it's not as useful as it currently is, while extracting as much value as we can now. One thing I worry about is if the lesson we take from this current window, where we have CoT that we can get something out of, is to iteratively do hacky fixes that slightly reduce rates, then we'll find ourselves in a year and a half with no longer much value from the CoT, and we didn't eliminate the problems we were seeing. I worry that I would plan for that trajectory.

I do think we should expect that chain of thought won't be around forever as a useful thing. You can imagine monitoring schemes where a model is trained to interpret the chain of thought on top of another model. If you look in recent papers on how much thinking models can do for a METR-style time horizon but just in a forward pass, it gets very high. By 2028, if we're at a 30-minute forward pass, the models might still need chain of thought, but 30 minutes is a long time. They don't have to come up with a whole plan in the forward pass; they just have to come up with, "How do I not sound catchably suspicious all the time in unambiguous ways?"

We need to plan for a world where we don't have chain of thought, or where it's not as useful as it currently is, while extracting as much value as we can now. One thing I worry about is if the lesson we take from this current window, where we have CoT that we can get something out of, is to iteratively do hacky fixes that slightly reduce rates, then we'll find ourselves in a year and a half with no longer much value from the CoT, and we didn't eliminate the problems we were seeing. I worry that I would plan for that trajectory.
